description: We are building a Single Page Application (SPA) to serve as a crew health "control center." The dashboard displays individual crew panels with a headshot, condition summary, and a status color (green, yellow, red, or gray for stale data). Clicking a panel instantly expands it to show body system tiles, actionable recommendations, and trend graphs.
summary:
Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

Our Team: More Gavish (Physics & Math, Technion); Yarin Nago (DevOps, healthcare startup); Mariam Hag (Biomedical Engineering & Medicine, Technion); Sabeel Saeed (Medical student); Amit Shirazi (Data Science, medical device startup).

On the way to Mars, messages can take 22 minutes each way, links can fail, and evacuation is impossible. Wearable sensors provide data, but readings are hard to interpret. Each astronaut has a different baseline, and space changes what “normal” means.

C.H.A.R.M. (Crew Health Assessment and Response Module) is a clinical decision-support app comparing readings with personal baselines and expected spaceflight changes. It provides four alert levels: NORMAL, ATTENTION, CAUTION, and CRITICAL, with next steps. Demos include infection, dehydration, SANS, and bone loss. Charmy, our AI assistant, reads guidance aloud. It works offline. In our demo, Sarah develops a respiratory infection, reaches CRITICAL, and receives onboard guidance when Earth contact is lost.

We combined ~20 NASA datasets and a simulated CSA stream into 88,735 measurements from 43 people, including bed-rest studies and Inspiration4 data. Our engine uses 26 clinically sourced alert rules, personal baselines, and space adaptations. NOAA data supports radiation alerts.

Our research uses real study-NASA participant and space-mission data. Scenarios are simulated; alert thresholds need clinical validation.
details:
What it does

As technology advances, humanity keeps reaching farther into space: back to the Moon, on to Mars, and beyond. Every step farther brings new challenges, and one of the hardest is independence. The farther a crew travels, the longer it waits for help from Earth. A message to Mars can take more than 20 minutes each way, and destinations beyond Mars mean hours. Sometimes there is no contact at all: when Artemis II flew behind the far side of the Moon, its crew was out of contact with Earth for about 40 minutes. In those moments, the crew must be able to assess their own health and act on their own.

C.H.A.R.M. (Crew Health Assessment and Response Module) is a clinical decision-support app built for exactly these moments. It helps astronauts notice health problems early and know what to do next, whether they are on a space station, in lunar orbit, on a lunar base or on the way to Mars. It keeps working when the link to Earth is delayed or down.

Each crew member has a health file. It shows vital signs, blood and exam results, sleep, mood, exercise, fluid intake, body mass and radiation dose. A body map shows which body system needs attention. Every measurement has a status shown as a colour, a word and a shape: NORMAL, ATTENTION, CAUTION or CRITICAL. NO DATA means the reading is missing or too old, and it is never shown as green.

For each alert, CHARM explains why it matters in space and gives the next step. Guided tests walk the astronaut through measurements one screen at a time, such as blood pressure, glucose, ECG and a reaction test. A daily mood and wellbeing check asks 14 short questions on a 1–5 scale, with room for the astronaut’s own notes. A routine task list reminds the crew what to measure each day. When someone becomes CRITICAL, Emergency Mode guides the crew step by step, with one illustrated, spoken screen per action for the Crew Medical Officer. Charmy, our AI Assistant, answers typed or spoken questions about the crew’s data and reads guidance aloud with a voice that runs on the device.

How it works

CHARM judges each reading in layers:

  • Clinical limits for everyone, from published criteria (NEWS2, SIRS/qSOFA, ADA, WHO, NASA standards).
  • The astronaut’s own baseline, from a statistical model fitted on real research data. The model adds the change expected in space for the current mission day.
  • Activity context. Exercise and sleep have their own limits.
  • Condition rules that combine several signals: bleeding, heart rhythm (vital signs set the urgency, and the ECG read by the medical officer names the rhythm), airway reaction to an airborne exposure, infection, dizziness on standing, low oxygen, circulation strain (shock index), kidney stone risk, neck-vein thrombosis, SANS (vision changes), space anemia and bone loss.
  • Trends over weeks, such as body-mass loss and a weekly vision self-test.

These rules come from 26 clinically sourced alert rules and our medic team’s scenario table. Personal limits can only add alerts, never remove them, and critical limits are the same for everyone. An alert clears only after the reading has stayed back in range for a while, so the status doesn’t flicker.

The same alert engine runs on the server and on every device. That keeps it working offline, and the screen always shows the same alerts the server raised. Every record is queued for the flight surgeon on Earth. The delay to Earth is calculated from the ship’s position. Our demo mission is a 6-month transfer to Mars, and the same model works for any destination.

Data comes from manual entry, guided tests, wearable streams, or CSV files from NASA, ESA, JAXA or CSA. Records are append-only and tagged REAL or SIMULATED.

Privacy:

  • Each astronaut sees only their own data, plus the status of their crewmates.
  • The flight surgeon sees every file.
  • In an emergency, a critical crewmate’s file opens to the crew, and the access is logged.

Data

We combined about 20 open NASA datasets and a simulated CSA dataset into 88,735 measurements from 43 people. Each measurement is traceable to its source:

  • NASA bed-rest studies, a ground analog of weightlessness
  • Inspiration4 blood counts from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository
  • A simulated CSA Bio-Monitor stream

Live NOAA space-weather data drives the solar radiation storm alerts. The crew characters are fictional, and their data comes from those research participants.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts get a quick, clear answer to “Is this normal for me, here, today?”, together with a concrete next step. They don’t need to be doctors or to watch dashboards all day. Personal baselines reduce false alarms for people whose normal is different, without hiding real danger.

The crew stays capable whenever Earth cannot answer in time. That can happen because of distance, or because the link is lost, as when a spacecraft passes behind the Moon. When the link returns, flight surgeons get a complete, prioritized record.

The same approach can support isolated places on Earth: Antarctic stations, ships at sea and remote clinics.

How it is creative

  • It adapts to each astronaut’s own baseline and to the mission day, instead of using one fixed limit.
  • It combines several signals into one condition alert with a clear next step.
  • It works across space agencies. CHARM reads health data in NASA, ESA, JAXA and CSA formats and turns it into one record and one alert system. An international crew shares one health tool, and every value keeps its source.
  • Charmy is a 3D assistant whose neural voice runs in the browser, with no server. Astronauts can also ask Charmy questions out loud.
  • The delay to Earth is calculated from orbital mechanics, not a fixed number.
  • Seven medic-team scenarios play live in the app: bleeding emergency, cardiac arrhythmia, airborne exposure / respiratory emergency, pulmonary infection, dehydration, SANS vision changes and bone loss. The measurements enter the astronaut’s file, and CHARM raises the alerts, the red alert and Emergency Mode by itself. Each scenario covers the whole path, including a stage where Earth is out of contact, through to recovery or long-term monitoring.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: CHARM is built on medical data and established clinical standards (NEWS2, SIRS/qSOFA, ADA, WHO and NASA’s SANS criteria). It does not replace a physician. It is the crew’s first line of assessment when no physician can answer in time: it catches problems early, guides the next step and hands the flight surgeon a complete record. Today, in-flight medical care still relies on real-time contact with the ground. Missions to the Moon and Mars will need a tool like CHARM.
  • Alarm fatigue: we tested the personal model on real data. It adds less than 2% extra alerts.
  • Communication delay and loss of contact: from about 40 minutes behind the Moon to tens of minutes or hours in deep space. CHARM works without a connection, and records queue for Earth.
  • Privacy between crewmates.
  • Accessibility: status is never shown by colour alone, touch targets are large enough for tablets, and Charmy can be used by voice.
  • Data provenance and integrity: values are tagged REAL or SIMULATED, and records are append-only.
  • Other agencies’ data formats.
  • Explainability: every alert shows which values triggered it, the rule behind it and the next step, so the crew and the flight surgeon can check CHARM’s reasoning instead of trusting a black box.

Tools and technologies

  • Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a single-page app with no build step). It runs on laptops, tablets and Android phones.
  • Backend: Firebase Hosting, Cloud Firestore with an offline cache, and Cloud Functions (Node.js 22).
  • Data and model: Python with pandas and NumPy, for the personal baselines (empirical Bayes), the space-adaptation curves and the evaluation.
  • Charmy: three.js for the 3D assistant. Piper text-to-speech runs in the browser through ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly). Spoken questions use the browser’s Web Speech API.
  • Testing and version control: the Node test runner, Git and Git LFS.
  • External data: NOAA SWPC space weather, NASA OSDR and NASA bed-rest data.
  • AI tools: Claude (Anthropic) helped with research, data processing, code and writing. Imagine.art was used to create the project video, and AI image tools were used for concept art. The team reviewed all outputs.
